messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Robert sat in his office at the middle school, the door closed, a stack of disciplinary referrals untouched on his desk. It was late afternoon, and the building was quiet except for the distant hum of the custodial crew. He had a meeting with a parent in ten minutes, and he was running through the conversation in his head for the fourth time: *First, ask about the student’s math grade. Then mention the attendance issue. Then pause. Wait for her response. Say something supportive but firm.* He could feel his jaw tightening. He had always been good with people, but that was before.

The life-threatening illness had arrived without warning two years ago, a bacterial infection that raged through his bloodstream so quickly that he barely remembered the ambulance ride or the ICU. He had been a widower for four years by then, and his job as a principal had been his anchor. But the infection had nearly killed him, and though he survived, something fundamental had been taken. When he tried to deliberately recall those hospital days, the details slipped away like water through a sieve. Yet sometimes, without any image, a wave of terror would crash over him—his heart pounding, his skin cold, his body stiffening as if he were again lying on that narrow gurney, unable to move, tubes and wires everywhere. He would feel his arms pinned to his sides, his neck locked, and he would have to shake himself to escape the position. The hospital smell—that sharp, antiseptic sting—could trigger it instantly. He had stopped walking past the clinic in town. He had not had a physical exam in over a year, ignoring the letters from his doctor. The thought of a needle or a stethoscope made his stomach clench.

The smell of alcohol was another thing. It reminded him of a night in the hospital, a visitor in the next bed who had been drinking, the sour odor mixing with disinfectant. Now, at school, if a parent or a teacher had even a hint of alcohol on their breath, Robert would feel his chest tighten and his mind go blank. He would excuse himself, retreat to his office, and sit in the dark until the feeling passed. He had begun to isolate more and more. Friends from before the illness—men he had golfed with, couples he and his wife had known—stopped calling because he never returned their calls. He told himself he didn't have the energy, that they wouldn't understand the person he had become. The person he had become was unrecognisable to him. He had been decisive, steady, the kind of principal who walked the halls with easy confidence. Now he second-guessed every word, every decision. He could no longer trust his own body—it had betrayed him once, and it could do so again without warning. So he rehearsed conversations before every meeting, before calling a parent, before even saying hello to the front office staff. It was exhausting, but it was the only way he felt he could keep from falling apart.

The cumulative weight of these strategies had hollowed out his life. His isolation meant he ate dinner alone most nights, watching television with the sound low. His avoidance of medical care meant he had not followed up on a recommended colonoscopy, and the thought of scheduling it made him nauseous. At work, he had started delegating tasks that required spontaneous interaction—morning announcements, assemblies—to his vice principal. The staff had noticed. A few had asked if he was okay, and he had smiled and said he was fine, but he could feel their eyes on him, and that only made him rehearse harder.

What finally brought Robert to a therapist’s office was a morning in late October. A student’s father, an alcoholic in recovery, had come to a conference smelling faintly of hand sanitizer, and Robert had frozen mid-sentence, then excused himself to the bathroom and vomited. He sat on the floor of the stall for fifteen minutes, his body locked in that familiar rigidity, his mind empty of any clear memory but flooded with the raw emotion of the ICU. That afternoon, he made the call. He was terrified that talking about his illness would make it real again, that he would lose the fragile control he had built. But he was also exhausted, and somewhere beneath the fear, he hoped that if he could untangle this knot, he might find the man he used to be.
